1359.title: Ramadan: the family
1359.hook: iftars with family, children's first fasts
1359.howItsDone: Muslim families gather for iftar at sunset during Ramadan, breaking the fast with dates and water as a report in Abu Dawud describes; children aren't required to fast before maturity, and some families let them practice with partial fasts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, planning Ramadan: reading, prayer, charity and rest, the column people forget. Today, the people around the table.

A small toy made of wool. Al-Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh, a woman of Madinah, describes it in Sahih al-Bukhari. Her people fasted, she says, and had their small children fast too. And they made toys out of wool for them. When one of the children cried for food, they'd hand over the toy, and the child would play with it until it was time to break the fast. No lecture. No scolding. A toy, and a little longer to wait.
screen: `A TOY MADE OF WOOL.` → `A CHILD CRIES FOR FOOD.` → `PLAY UNTIL SUNSET.`

segments.voice: First, be honest about the report. Al-Rubayyi' is speaking about the fast of Ashura, not Ramadan. But it gives a picture of how children were brought into a fast: gently, with play, alongside the adults. Children aren't required to fast before they come of age, as you met earlier on the path, so a child's first fast is practice, not duty. Some families start with half a day, or a fast that ends at lunch, and make a fuss of the child at sunset. Second, the moment the fast breaks. In al-Bukhari the Prophet, peace be upon him, says people will remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast. When the sun goes down, you eat. And in a report in Abu Dawud, Anas describes how: with fresh dates before the prayer, and if there were none, dried dates, and if there were none, a few sips of water. So the iftar starts small and sweet, and for some families the big meal comes after. Third, the table. For some families, iftar is the one meal of the day when everyone is home at the same minute, because the sun decides the time, not anyone's schedule. Grandparents, cousins, the kid who just finished a half-day fast and wants everyone to know. Put the toy and the date side by side. Both are small. Both say the fast is hard, and the family's job is to make it bearable, together, until the moment it's sweet.
screen: `A CHILD'S FAST IS PRACTICE.` · `HURRY TO BREAK THE FAST.` · `DATES, THEN WATER.` · `EVERYONE HOME AT ONE MINUTE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child in your life, a son or daughter, a niece, a neighbor's kid, or the child you once were, and think of one way they could share in something you care about, sized to them: a job at the table, handing out the dates, saying the first thing at a meal. Picture their face when they're trusted with it. If you pray, you can remember that child by name.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, kept at home around the iftar table, where children practice small fasts and the day breaks with dates. Today's word.
Your line: the family fasts. Small and sweet, together. Same time tomorrow.

1360.title: Ramadan: the mosque
1360.howItsDone: In Ramadan, mosques may hold a congregational night prayer called tarawih, which reports in al-Bukhari trace to 'Umar gathering people behind one reciter, and some host iftars at sunset open to anyone, following a hadith in al-Tirmidhi on the reward of feeding a fasting person; Shia Muslims keep Ramadan nights with their own prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramadan at home: a toy of wool, dates at sunset, everyone at the table at once. Today, down the street.

Late one night in Ramadan, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, goes out to the mosque in Madinah and prays. A few men see him and pray behind him. The next night, more people come, and the next, more again, until the mosque is full of people waiting for him. 'A'ishah tells it in Sahih al-Bukhari. Then, one night, he doesn't come out. They wait. He stays home. At the dawn prayer, he explains why.
screen: `HE PRAYS ALONE AT NIGHT.` → `EACH NIGHT, MORE PEOPLE.` → `ONE NIGHT, HE STAYS HOME.`

segments.voice: His explanation, in paraphrase: your being there was not hidden from me, but I was afraid this prayer would be made obligatory on you, and you wouldn't be able to keep it up. He stayed home out of mercy, to keep a voluntary prayer voluntary. The night prayer of Ramadan began as a gift, and he protected it from becoming a burden. Al-Bukhari also reports that later, in the time of 'Umar, he walked into the mosque one Ramadan night and found people praying scattered, some alone, some in small groups behind one man. He gathered them into one congregation behind a single reciter, Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Another night he saw them praying together and said, in paraphrase, what a fine new thing this is. That gathered night prayer came to be called tarawih, which you first met in year one. Schools differ on how long it should be, and not every community prays it in congregation. Shia Muslims, for example, keep Ramadan nights with their own prayers. Before the prayer, the food. In a hadith in al-Tirmidhi, whoever gives a fasting person food to break the fast has a reward like theirs, without the fasting person's reward being reduced at all. So some mosques open their doors at sunset: long sheets on the floor, volunteers carrying trays, dates, water, soup, rice, strangers passing plates to strangers. The family table seats the people who share your house. The mosque table seats whoever walks in: the student far from home, the new neighbor, the person who would otherwise break the fast alone. Ramadan widens the table.
screen: `HE STAYED HOME, OUT OF MERCY.` · `'UMAR GATHERS ONE CONGREGATION.` · `FEED A FASTING PERSON.` · `RAMADAN WIDENS THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Picture a long cloth on a mosque floor at sunset, plates going down the line, and someone you don't know beside you, passing you a date. Then think whether a mosque near you holds an iftar open to guests, or, if you don't go to a mosque, of one person who eats alone and how you might share a meal. If you pray, you can remember the people who cook and serve.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, kept in the mosque with the night prayer called tarawih and with iftars where whoever walks in gets fed. Today's word.
Your line: the community table. Whoever walks in gets fed. Rest well.

1361.title: Ramadan: the last ten
1361.hook: the Prophet ﷺ tightened his belt and woke his family in the last ten (Bukhari)
1361.howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, Muslims add night prayer and look for the Night of Power in the odd nights, as hadiths in al-Bukhari describe; some stay in the mosque in a retreat called i'tikaf, and some repeat the short prayer for pardon the Prophet taught 'A'ishah, kept in al-Tirmidhi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mosque in Ramadan: a night prayer kept voluntary out of mercy, and a table where whoever walks in gets fed. Today, the end of the month, when things speed up.

In everyday English, tightening your belt means cutting back. Spending less. Getting by. In a report from 'A'ishah in Sahih al-Bukhari, it means almost the opposite. She describes what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, did when the last ten nights of Ramadan began. In paraphrase: he tightened his waist-wrapper, he brought his nights to life, and he woke his family. Not cutting back. Gearing up. The month was nearly over, and instead of coasting toward the finish, he went harder.
screen: `TIGHTENING YOUR BELT: CUTTING BACK?` → `HE TIGHTENED HIS WAIST-WRAPPER.` → `GEARING UP, NOT COASTING.`

segments.voice: Take her three phrases one at a time. He tightened his waist-wrapper: scholars read this two ways. Some say it means serious effort, the way a worker cinches a belt before lifting. Others say he withdrew from his wives for those nights to give himself to worship. Some hold both. He brought his nights to life: he stayed awake in prayer instead of sleeping through them. And he woke his family. He didn't keep the nights to himself. Why these nights? The Qur'an names a night, the Night of Power, which you first met in year one. Surah al-Qadr says, in Pickthall's words: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." In another report in al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells people to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten. The report names no single night, so the way to find it is to show up for all of them. Some go further and stay in the mosque. 'A'ishah says in al-Bukhari that he kept i'tikaf, a retreat in the mosque, in the last ten, and his wives kept it after him. And what to say if you find the night? In al-Tirmidhi, 'A'ishah asks him exactly that. He teaches her a short prayer asking Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon. Not for wealth. Not for a sign. For pardon. So the last ten have a shape: effort, wakefulness, family, retreat, and at the center, one plain request.
screen: `THREE THINGS 'A'ISHAH SAW.` · `THE NIGHT OF POWER, UNNAMED.` · `I'TIKAF: A RETREAT IN THE MOSQUE.` · `AT THE CENTER, ASKING PARDON.`

segments.voice: Choose a night, in Ramadan if you keep it or any night this week if you don't, and picture the alarm going off in the dark, the house quiet, and you sitting up instead of rolling over. What would you do with that hour: pray, read, sit in silence, write down what you're sorry for and thankful for? If you pray, you can ask for pardon, the way the Prophet taught 'A'ishah.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, which ends in ten nights of extra effort, with the Night of Power hidden somewhere among them. Today's word.
Your line: tighten the belt. Gearing up, not coasting, at the very end. Until tomorrow.

1362.title: Eid al-Fitr: the day
1362.hook: ghusl, perfume, best clothes, eating before prayer, a different road back (Bukhari)
1362.howItsDone: On the morning of Eid al-Fitr, Muslims often bathe, put on their best clothes, eat a few dates, and go to the Eid prayer together, and some take a different road home afterward, following a report in Sahih al-Bukhari.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last ten nights of Ramadan: the Prophet tightened his belt, brought the nights to life and woke his family. Now the month is over.

A small detail, tucked into Sahih al-Bukhari, in a report from Jabir. On the day of Eid, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, went out to the prayer by one road and came home by another. That's the whole report. No reason given. Just two roads. Before that walk, there's a morning to get through: water, clothes, something sweet to eat. Today, the morning of Eid al-Fitr, the feast that breaks the fast, one small act at a time.
screen: `ONE ROAD OUT.` → `ANOTHER ROAD BACK.` → `NO REASON GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Start with water. In the Muwatta of Imam Malik, Ibn 'Umar, a companion of the Prophet, would take a full bath, a ghusl, on the morning of the Fitr before going out to the prayer. The day begins clean. Then clothes. In al-Bukhari, 'Umar finds a fine cloak in the market and brings it to the Prophet, saying, in paraphrase: buy this, and dress up in it for Eid and for receiving visitors. The Prophet turned that one down, because it was silk. But notice what 'Umar took for granted: Eid is a day you dress for. For some, a little perfume too. Then food, and here's the surprise. Anas reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet would not go out on the day of the Fitr until he had eaten some dates, in an odd number. For a month, every fast broke at sunset. This one breaks in daylight, on purpose, before the prayer. Then the prayer itself, together with everyone. And then the road home, the different one. Why? Scholars have offered reasons: so both roads see the people of the day, so more neighbors get greeted, so more ground bears witness to the prayer. But Jabir only tells us what he did. The meaning is left open.
screen: `WATER: A GHUSL BEFORE GOING OUT.` · `CLOTHES: A DAY YOU DRESS FOR.` · `DATES BEFORE THE PRAYER.` · `A DIFFERENT ROAD HOME.`

segments.voice: In your mind, trace the way you usually come home: the turns, the corners, the same doors you've stopped noticing. Now find one other way, one street over or the long way round the park, and picture who might be on that road whom you never pass. If you pray, keep the Eid morning walk in mind; if you don't, simply keep the new road ready.
Eid al-Fitr. The feast that breaks the fast of Ramadan: a bath, good clothes, dates before the prayer, and a different road back. Today's word.
Your line: a new road home. The second road is still there to walk. See you tomorrow.

1363.title: Dhul Qa'dah
1363.howItsDone: In Dhul Qa'dah, Muslims preparing for hajj often settle debts, ask forgiveness of family and friends, and gather their simple white garments, and families and mosques send them off with prayers for a safe journey.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eid al-Fitr: a bath, good clothes, dates before the prayer, and a different road home.

A suitcase lies open on a bed, half full. Two lengths of plain white cloth, folded. A small bottle of unscented soap. A list on the fridge of people to call before leaving: an aunt, an old friend, a neighbor they once argued with. Someone in this house is going on hajj. The calendar has turned to Dhul Qa'dah, one of the sacred months from earlier on the path. Nothing big happens in it on the calendar. But in houses like this one, bags are being packed.
screen: `A SUITCASE, HALF FULL.` → `PEOPLE TO CALL BEFORE LEAVING.` → `BAGS BEING PACKED.`

segments.voice: First, it sits inside the season of the pilgrimage. Surah al-Baqarah says, in Pickthall's translation: "The pilgrimage is (in) the well-known months." Tradition counts Dhul Qa'dah among them, so travelers can already be on the road. Second, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, chose this month for his own journeys to Makkah. Anas reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet's 'umrahs, the lesser pilgrimages, were in Dhul Qa'dah, except the one he joined to his hajj. Third, packing. The same verse goes on: "So make provision for yourselves (Hereafter); for the best provision is to ward off evil." Pack your bag, it says, and then it names a provision no bag can hold. So for some pilgrims, getting ready means paying back what they owe and asking forgiveness from people they've wronged: the calls on the fridge list. Fourth, the people who stay. In al-Tirmidhi, when someone was leaving, the Prophet would say, in paraphrase: I entrust to Allah your religion, what you've been trusted with, and the last of your deeds. Not a wish for good weather. A handing over.
screen: `THE WELL-KNOWN MONTHS.` · `THE PROPHET'S 'UMRAHS.` · `THE BEST PROVISION.` · `HANDING THE TRAVELER OVER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is going on hajj, or has gone, or hopes to go someday; if no one comes, picture a stranger in white at an airport gate, a little nervous, passport in hand. Stay with their packing and their goodbyes for a few breaths. If you pray, use the Prophet's farewell, I entrust you to Allah; if not, wish them a safe road and a good return.
Dhul Qa'dah. A sacred month, the month before the hajj, when the Prophet made his 'umrahs and when pilgrims pack, settle their debts and say their goodbyes. Today's word.
Your line: the pilgrims set out. And the ones at home hand them over. Tomorrow, Dhul Hijjah at home.

1364.title: Dhul Hijjah at home
1364.hook: many who plan to sacrifice don't cut hair or nails in the first ten (Muslim)
1364.howItsDone: In the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah, Muslims at home often increase prayer, charity and takbir, and some fast on the day of 'Arafah; those who intend to offer a sacrifice for Eid al-Adha often leave their hair and nails uncut until it is done, following a hadith in Sahih Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhul Qa'dah: bags packed, debts settled, and the traveler handed over to Allah.

The new moon of Dhul Hijjah is sighted. Far away, the pilgrims are in Makkah in their white cloth. And in an ordinary house, a pair of nail clippers goes into a drawer and stays there. A haircut gets moved to later in the month. Nobody here is on hajj. So why is someone at home suddenly not cutting their nails? It goes back to one hadith, and to a question anyone who stays behind might ask: how do I take part in a journey I'm not on?
screen: `THE NEW MOON OF DHUL HIJJAH.` → `CLIPPERS IN A DRAWER.` → `TAKING PART FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Umm Salamah, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reports his words in Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase: when the ten days begin, and one of you intends to offer a sacrifice, let him leave his hair and his skin alone. A small holding back, for someone planning the sacrifice of the coming Eid. Schools of law differ on how binding it is: some treat it as required, some as recommended, and some don't require it. Why it matters: pilgrims in ihram have their own list of things they leave alone, and cutting hair and nails is on it. Some scholars point out the echo. At home, a person keeps one small piece of what the pilgrim keeps. Then the days themselves. In al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Abbas reports the Prophet saying, in paraphrase, that no good deeds are dearer to Allah than those done in these ten days. They asked: not even striving in Allah's path? Not even that, he said, except a person who goes out with himself and his wealth and comes back with nothing. Days for everyone, not only travelers. And a sound you might hear: al-Bukhari mentions that Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayrah would go out to the market in these days saying Allahu akbar, and people said it with them. On the day of 'Arafah, when the pilgrims stand on the plain, some at home fast. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet's hope that this fast wipes away the sins of the year before it and the year after.
screen: `LEAVE HAIR AND NAILS ALONE.` · `AN ECHO OF THE PILGRIM'S IHRAM.` · `NO DEEDS DEARER THAN IN THESE DAYS.` · `TAKBIR IN THE MARKET, A FAST AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Choose one tiny thing to leave alone for a while: hitting snooze, a purchase you don't need, a comment you'd usually make. Each time you notice yourself not doing it, let that moment point to someone far away who is keeping much more. If you pray, remember the pilgrims each time; if not, notice the space the small restraint opens up.

1365.title: Eid al-Adha: the day
1365.hook: the prayer, the sacrifice, the sharing, the visits
1365.howItsDone: On Eid al-Adha, Muslims go to the Eid prayer, and afterward those who can afford it offer an animal in sacrifice, or pay for one to be offered, and share its meat with family, friends and people in need; the day is also for visiting relatives and neighbors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhul Hijjah at home: clippers in a drawer, a small restraint kept for pilgrims far away.

"Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." A line from Surah al-Hajj, in Pickthall's translation, and a strange thing to say on the morning of a sacrifice. The animal is real. The knife is real. The meat will be cooked and eaten by nightfall. And the verse says none of that is what reaches Allah. Something else does. Today, Eid al-Adha, the feast of the sacrifice, and a morning with an order to it.
screen: `THEIR FLESH AND BLOOD REACH NOT ALLAH.` → `THE DEVOTION REACHES HIM.` → `AN ORDER TO THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: First, the prayer. Al-Bara' reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase: the first thing we do on this day of ours is pray, then go back and sacrifice. The sacrifice comes after the prayer, not before. Second, the sacrifice. The Qur'an tells of Ibrahim, ready to give up his son, and then: "Then We ransomed him with a tremendous victim." The animal stands where the son stood. Families who can afford it offer a sheep, a goat, a cow or a share in a camel, or pay for one to be offered on their behalf. Third, where the meat goes. The same surah says of the animals: "eat thereof and feed the beggar and the suppliant." Eat, and feed. Some scholars recommend dividing it: some for the household, some for relatives and friends, some for those in need. The feast is not kept whole. Fourth, the visits. The rest of the day, and the days after, people go from house to house, carry plates to neighbors, sit with the old aunt they don't see enough. Prayer, then the knife, then the plate, then the door. The devotion is what reaches Allah. The meat goes the other way, out across the street, into other people's kitchens.
screen: `FIRST THE PRAYER, THEN THE SACRIFICE.` · `AN ANIMAL WHERE THE SON STOOD.` · `EAT, AND FEED.` · `HOUSE TO HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Think of what you'll eat today or later this week, and picture one plate of it going out the door instead of onto your table. Who gets it: a neighbor you only wave at, a friend having a hard month, someone living alone? If you pray, remember the verse, the devotion is what reaches Him; if not, just hold the picture of the plate in someone else's hands.
Eid al-Adha. The feast of the sacrifice at the height of the hajj: prayer first, then the sacrifice, then the meat shared out, then the visits. Today's word.
